claim: W3 ganglion cells are the most abundant ganglion cell type in mice.
source: The most abundant RGC type in the mouse retina (W3-RGC) was recently shown to respond selectively to movements of small—in terms of size on the retina—objects (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2012

claim: W3 ganglion cells selectively respond to movements of small objects.
source: The most abundant RGC type in the mouse retina (W3-RGC) was recently shown to respond selectively to movements of small—in terms of size on the retina—objects (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2012

claim: VGluT3-expressing amacrine cells are object motion sensitive.
source: We find that these ACs are object motion sensitive and analyze the synaptic mechanisms underlying this computation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 2-photon-guided patch-clamp recordings presented in the manuscript

claim: VGluT3-expressing amacrine cells form glutamatergic synapses with W3 ganglion cells.
source: Anatomical circuit reconstructions suggest that VGluT3-expressing ACs form glutamatergic synapses with W3 ganglion cells, and targeted recordings show that the tuning of W3 ganglion cells' excitatory input matches that of VGluT3-expressing ACs' responses.
evidence: Supported by anatomical circuit reconstruction data presented in the manuscript

claim: The tuning of W3 ganglion cells' excitatory input matches that of VGluT3-expressing amacrine cells' responses.
source: Anatomical circuit reconstructions suggest that VGluT3-expressing ACs form glutamatergic synapses with W3 ganglion cells, and targeted recordings show that the tuning of W3 ganglion cells' excitatory input matches that of VGluT3-expressing ACs' responses.
evidence: Supported by targeted recording data presented in the manuscript

claim: Synaptic excitation of W3 ganglion cells is diminished in mice lacking VGluT3.
source: Synaptic excitation of W3 ganglion cells is diminished, and responses to object motion are suppressed in mice lacking VGluT3.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from VGluT3 knockout mice presented in the manuscript

claim: Responses to object motion are suppressed in W3 ganglion cells in mice lacking VGluT3.
source: Synaptic excitation of W3 ganglion cells is diminished, and responses to object motion are suppressed in mice lacking VGluT3.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from VGluT3 knockout mice presented in the manuscript

claim: Object motion is first detected by VGluT3-expressing amacrine cells.
source: Object motion, thus, is first detected by VGluT3-expressing ACs, which provide feature-selective excitatory input to W3 ganglion cells.
evidence: Supported by inference from experimental data showing VG3-ACs are object motion sensitive and provide excitatory input to W3-RGCs

claim: VGluT3-expressing amacrine cells provide feature-selective excitatory input to W3 ganglion cells.
source: Object motion, thus, is first detected by VGluT3-expressing ACs, which provide feature-selective excitatory input to W3 ganglion cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing matching tuning properties and reduced responses in VGluT3 knockout mice

claim: Head, body, and eye movements frequently shift the retinal image.
source: Detecting object motion is a challenging task as head, body, and eye movements frequently shift the retinal image (Martinez-Conde et al., 2004; Sakatani and Isa, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Martinez-Conde et al., 2004 and Sakatani and Isa, 2007

claim: Object motion sensitive RGCs respond to differences in the timing of texture movements in their receptive field center and surround.
source: To distinguish movements of objects and the background, object motion sensitive (OMS) RGCs respond to differences in the timing of texture movements in their receptive field center and surround (Olveczky et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Olveczky et al., 2003 and Zhang et al., 2012

claim: W3-RGCs share key properties with OMS RGCs in rabbit and salamander.
source: W3-RGCs share key properties with OMS RGCs in rabbit and salamander, but, due to stronger surround suppression, do not respond at the border of larger objects (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2012

claim: W3-RGCs do not respond at the border of larger objects due to stronger surround suppression.
source: W3-RGCs share key properties with OMS RGCs in rabbit and salamander, but, due to stronger surround suppression, do not respond at the border of larger objects (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2012

claim: Key response properties of W3-RGCs appear to be inherited from their excitatory input.
source: Although postsynaptic inhibition and spike thresholds sharpen the tuning of W3-RGCs, similar to other OMS and local-edge-detector RGCs, key response properties appear to be inherited from their excitatory input (van Wyk et al., 2006; Baccus et al., 2008; Russell and Werblin, 2010; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to van Wyk et al., 2006; Baccus et al., 2008; Russell and Werblin, 2010; Zhang et al., 2012

claim: Feature selectivity arises presynaptic to W3-RGCs.
source: This suggests that feature selectivity arises presynaptic to W3-RGCs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that key response properties are inherited from excitatory input

claim: RGCs typically receive excitatory input from bipolar cells.
source: Typically, RGCs receive excitatory input from bipolar cells (Euler et al., 2014) and inhibitory input from amacrine cells (ACs).
evidence: Supported by citation to Euler et al., 2014

claim: RGCs typically receive inhibitory input from amacrine cells.
source: Typically, RGCs receive excitatory input from bipolar cells (Euler et al., 2014) and inhibitory input from amacrine cells (ACs).
evidence: Represents established scientific knowledge about retinal circuitry

claim: Amacrine cells are the most diverse class of neurons in the retina.
source: ACs are the most diverse class of neurons in the retina, encompassing 30–50 cell types (MacNeil and Masland, 1998; Helmstaedter et al., 2013) that serve task-specific functions in vision (Dacheux and Raviola, 1986; Yoshida et al., 2001; Euler et al., 2002; Munch et al., 2009; Grimes et al., 2010; Chen and Li, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to MacNeil and Masland, 1998 and Helmstaedter et al., 2013

claim: The retina contains 30-50 amacrine cell types.
source: ACs are the most diverse class of neurons in the retina, encompassing 30–50 cell types (MacNeil and Masland, 1998; Helmstaedter et al., 2013) that serve task-specific functions in vision (Dacheux and Raviola, 1986; Yoshida et al., 2001; Euler et al., 2002; Munch et al., 2009; Grimes et al., 2010; Chen and Li, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to MacNeil and Masland, 1998 and Helmstaedter et al., 2013

claim: Amacrine cells serve task-specific functions in vision.
source: ACs are the most diverse class of neurons in the retina, encompassing 30–50 cell types (MacNeil and Masland, 1998; Helmstaedter et al., 2013) that serve task-specific functions in vision (Dacheux and Raviola, 1986; Yoshida et al., 2001; Euler et al., 2002; Munch et al., 2009; Grimes et al., 2010; Chen and Li, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Most amacrine cells release GABA or glycine.
source: Although most ACs release γ-Aminobutyric acid (GABA) or glycine, a wide range of neurotransmitters and neuromodulators can be found in different cell types including one expressing the vesicular glutamate transporter 3 (VGluT3) (gene: Slc17a8, protein: VGluT3, AC: VG3) (Fyk-Kolodziej et al., 2004; Haverkamp and Wassle, 2004; Johnson et al., 2004).
evidence: Represents established knowledge about amacrine cell neurotransmitters

claim: VG3-ACs are conserved from rodents to primates.
source: VG3-ACs are conserved from rodents to primates.
evidence: Represents established knowledge about VG3-AC conservation across species

claim: VG3-ACs respond to light increments (ON) and decrements (OFF).
source: Recent studies found that VG3-ACs respond to light increments (ON) and decrements (OFF) (Grimes et al., 2011), show strong surround suppression, and following optogenetic or electrical stimulation can release glutamate (Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grimes et al., 2011

claim: VG3-ACs show strong surround suppression.
source: Recent studies found that VG3-ACs respond to light increments (ON) and decrements (OFF) (Grimes et al., 2011), show strong surround suppression, and following optogenetic or electrical stimulation can release glutamate (Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2014

claim: VG3-ACs can release glutamate following optogenetic or electrical stimulation.
source: Recent studies found that VG3-ACs respond to light increments (ON) and decrements (OFF) (Grimes et al., 2011), show strong surround suppression, and following optogenetic or electrical stimulation can release glutamate (Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2014

claim: VG3-ACs have a mean territory size of 7662 ± 211 μm².
source: Neurites of VG3-ACs stratify broadly in the center of the inner plexiform layer (Grimes et al., 2011), occupy medium-sized lateral territories (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, 7662 ± 211 μm2, n = 39), and as a population, cover the retina approximately seven times (coverage: 6.88).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements from 39 cells shown in Figure 1A

claim: VG3-ACs stratify broadly in the center of the inner plexiform layer.
source: Neurites of VG3-ACs stratify broadly in the center of the inner plexiform layer (Grimes et al., 2011), occupy medium-sized lateral territories (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, 7662 ± 211 μm2, n = 39), and as a population, cover the retina approximately seven times (coverage: 6.88).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grimes et al., 2011

claim: VG3-ACs as a population cover the retina approximately seven times.
source: Neurites of VG3-ACs stratify broadly in the center of the inner plexiform layer (Grimes et al., 2011), occupy medium-sized lateral territories (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, 7662 ± 211 μm2, n = 39), and as a population, cover the retina approximately seven times (coverage: 6.88).
evidence: Supported by experimental data calculating coverage factor

claim: VG3-ACs respond transiently to light increments and decrements.
source: Consistent with previous results, we find that VG3-ACs respond transiently to light increments and decrements, depolarizing to small and hyperpolarizing to large stimuli (Lee et al., 2014) (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C and citation to Lee et al., 2014

claim: VG3-ACs depolarize to small stimuli and hyperpolarize to large stimuli.
source: Consistent with previous results, we find that VG3-ACs respond transiently to light increments and decrements, depolarizing to small and hyperpolarizing to large stimuli (Lee et al., 2014) (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C and citation to Lee et al., 2014

claim: The switch in response polarity in VG3-ACs is caused by a combination of pre- and post-synaptic surround inhibition.
source: Voltage-clamp recordings revealed that this switch in response polarity is caused by a combination of pre- and post-synaptic surround inhibition (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: Supported by voltage-clamp recording data shown in Figure 1D-F

claim: Excitatory and voltage-response receptive fields of VG3-ACs are well fit by Difference-of-Gaussians models.
source: Excitatory and voltage-response receptive fields are well fit by Difference-of-Gaussians models (Enroth-Cugell and Robson, 1966; McMahon et al., 2004), whereas a single Gaussian is sufficient to describe the monotonic rise of inhibition with stimulus size.
evidence: Supported by experimental data fitting and citations to Enroth-Cugell and Robson, 1966 and McMahon et al., 2004

claim: A single Gaussian is sufficient to describe the monotonic rise of inhibition with stimulus size in VG3-ACs.
source: Excitatory and voltage-response receptive fields are well fit by Difference-of-Gaussians models (Enroth-Cugell and Robson, 1966; McMahon et al., 2004), whereas a single Gaussian is sufficient to describe the monotonic rise of inhibition with stimulus size.
evidence: Supported by experimental data fitting

claim: For VG3-ACs, OFF responses exceed ON responses for all components.
source: For all components, OFF responses exceed ON responses, and for voltage responses and excitatory inputs, ON receptive fields are larger in diameter than their OFF counterparts.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from receptive field measurements

claim: For VG3-ACs, ON receptive fields are larger in diameter than OFF receptive fields for voltage responses and excitatory inputs.
source: For all components, OFF responses exceed ON responses, and for voltage responses and excitatory inputs, ON receptive fields are larger in diameter than their OFF counterparts.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from receptive field measurements

claim: The resting membrane potential of VG3-ACs is −38 ± 1.2 mV.
source: The resting membrane potential of VG3-ACs in our recordings was −38 ± 1.2 mV (n = 26).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements from 26 cells

claim: VG3-ACs receive rectified excitatory input from transient ON and OFF bipolar cells.
source: Thus, VG3-ACs receive rectified excitatory input from transient ON and OFF bipolar cells, and inhibition from ACs, which themselves appear to be driven by rectified input from possibly the same types of bipolar cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from split-field stimulation experiments

claim: VG3-ACs receive inhibition from amacrine cells that are driven by rectified input from bipolar cells.
source: Thus, VG3-ACs receive rectified excitatory input from transient ON and OFF bipolar cells, and inhibition from ACs, which themselves appear to be driven by rectified input from possibly the same types of bipolar cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from counter-phase grating experiments

claim: VG3-ACs depolarize robustly to differential motion in the center.
source: When square-wave gratings overlaying center and surround regions of their receptive field were shifted separately or together (Figure 2A) (Baccus et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2012), VG3-ACs depolarized robustly to differential motion in the center, but hyperpolarized to synchronous movements in center and surround (i.e., global motion) and differential motion in the surround (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,C

claim: VG3-ACs hyperpolarize to global motion.
source: When square-wave gratings overlaying center and surround regions of their receptive field were shifted separately or together (Figure 2A) (Baccus et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2012), VG3-ACs depolarized robustly to differential motion in the center, but hyperpolarized to synchronous movements in center and surround (i.e., global motion) and differential motion in the surround (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,C

claim: VG3-ACs hyperpolarize to differential motion in the surround.
source: When square-wave gratings overlaying center and surround regions of their receptive field were shifted separately or together (Figure 2A) (Baccus et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2012), VG3-ACs depolarized robustly to differential motion in the center, but hyperpolarized to synchronous movements in center and surround (i.e., global motion) and differential motion in the surround (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,C

claim: VG3-ACs show preferential excitation during center-only motion.
source: Voltage-clamp recordings revealed that this response pattern is caused by preferential excitation during center-only motion and strong inhibition elicited whenever motion includes the surround (Figure 2B,E,D).
evidence: Supported by voltage-clamp recording data shown in Figure 2B,E,D

claim: VG3-ACs receive strong inhibition whenever motion includes the surround.
source: Voltage-clamp recordings revealed that this response pattern is caused by preferential excitation during center-only motion and strong inhibition elicited whenever motion includes the surround (Figure 2B,E,D).
evidence: Supported by voltage-clamp recording data shown in Figure 2B,E,D

claim: VG3-ACs can detect when an object moves at a different time than the background irrespective of the precise spatial patterns involved.
source: Since the average luminance in center and surround regions does not change in this stimulus, the observed responses provide further evidence that both are composed of rectified subunits, allowing VG3-ACs to detect when an object moves at a different time than the background irrespective of the precise spatial patterns involved, a defining feature of OMS neurons (Olveczky et al., 2003; Baccus et al., 2008).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on differential motion responses and citation to Olveczky et al., 2003 and Baccus et al., 2008

claim: Narrow dark bars moving across VG3-AC receptive fields elicit transient depolarizations as leading and trailing edges cross the receptive field center.
source: Narrow dark bars moving across the receptive fields of VG3-ACs elicited transient depolarizations as leading and trailing edges cross the receptive field center.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from moving bar experiments

claim: Robust edge responses in VG3-ACs were observed over a wide range of motion speeds.
source: Robust edge responses were observed over a wide range of motion speeds (Figure 2G,H) and were indistinguishable for leading and trailing edges in spite of the opposite polarity of the associated temporal contrast.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G,H

claim: Edge responses in VG3-ACs were indistinguishable for leading and trailing edges despite opposite polarity of temporal contrast.
source: Robust edge responses were observed over a wide range of motion speeds (Figure 2G,H) and were indistinguishable for leading and trailing edges in spite of the opposite polarity of the associated temporal contrast.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G,H

claim: VG3-AC responses are not directionally selective.
source: Responses of VG3-ACs are not directionally selective (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Edge responses in VG3-ACs were strongly suppressed for bar heights above 200 μm.
source: Edge responses were strongly suppressed for bar heights above 200 μm (Figure 2L,M).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2L,M

claim: Surround suppression of VG3-ACs is mediated by spiking amacrine cells.
source: To test whether surround suppression of VG3-ACs is similarly mediated by spiking ACs and to assess its importance to feature detection, we tested the effect of the sodium channel blocker TTX on VG3-ACs' responses in differential motion and edge detection stimulus paradigms.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing TTX abolishes surround suppression

claim: In the presence of TTX, VG3-ACs depolarize to global motion as well as differential center motion.
source: In the presence of TTX, VG3-ACs depolarized to global motion as well as differential center motion, and hyperpolarizations observed during surround stimulation were abolished (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B

claim: TTX abolishes hyperpolarizations observed during surround stimulation in VG3-ACs.
source: In the presence of TTX, VG3-ACs depolarized to global motion as well as differential center motion, and hyperpolarizations observed during surround stimulation were abolished (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B

claim: Edge responses elicited by narrow bars moving across VG3-AC receptive fields were not changed by TTX.
source: Edge responses elicited by narrow bars moving across the receptive fields of VG3-ACs at a variety of speeds were not changed by TTX (Figure 3C,D), but the suppression observed for larger bars was blocked (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D

claim: TTX blocks the suppression of edge responses observed for larger bars in VG3-ACs.
source: Edge responses elicited by narrow bars moving across the receptive fields of VG3-ACs at a variety of speeds were not changed by TTX (Figure 3C,D), but the suppression observed for larger bars was blocked (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E,F

claim: Surround inhibition is critical for the feature detection of VG3-ACs.
source: Surround inhibition, thus, is critical for the feature detection of VG3-ACs and appears to be mediated by spiking ACs.
evidence: Inferred from TTX experiments showing loss of feature selectivity

claim: The use of spikes to signal surround motion likely improves temporal coincidence of inhibitory input with bipolar cell depolarization.
source: The use of spikes to signal surround motion likely improves temporal coincidence of inhibitory input with bipolar cell depolarization and excitatory input to VG3-ACs during coherent motion, leading to more effective cancellation of center signals by the surround.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the functional advantage of spiking inhibition

claim: More than half of the PSD95-YFP puncta on W3-RGCs were apposed by VG3-AC boutons.
source: More than half of the PSD95-YFP puncta on W3-RGCs were apposed by VG3-ACs boutons, whereas few appositions with VG3-ACs were observed when PSD95-YFP puncta were randomly repositioned along the dendrites in Monte Carlo simulations (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 4C,D

claim: Few appositions between PSD95-YFP puncta and VG3-ACs were observed when puncta were randomly repositioned in Monte Carlo simulations.
source: More than half of the PSD95-YFP puncta on W3-RGCs were apposed by VG3-ACs boutons, whereas few appositions with VG3-ACs were observed when PSD95-YFP puncta were randomly repositioned along the dendrites in Monte Carlo simulations (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by Monte Carlo simulation data shown in Figure 4C,D

claim: W3-RGCs have small dendritic fields with territory size of 10,783 ± 409 μm².
source: W3-RGCs were identified by their characteristic morphology (Kim et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2012) with small dendritic fields (territory size: 10,783 ± 409 μm2, n = 25) filled by densely branched neurites stratifying in the center of the IPL with a secondary arborization near the border between the inner plexiform and inner nuclear layers (INLs).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements from 25 cells

claim: W3-RGC neurites stratify in the center of the IPL with a secondary arborization near the border between the inner plexiform and inner nuclear layers.
source: W3-RGCs were identified by their characteristic morphology (Kim et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2012) with small dendritic fields (territory size: 10,783 ± 409 μm2, n = 25) filled by densely branched neurites stratifying in the center of the IPL with a secondary arborization near the border between the inner plexiform and inner nuclear layers (INLs).
evidence: Supported by anatomical observations and citations to Kim et al., 2010 and Zhang et al., 2012

claim: W3-RGC EPSCs in VGluT3−/− mice were significantly reduced compared to WT littermates during differential center motion.
source: W3-RGC EPSCs in VGluT3−/− mice were significantly reduced compared to WT littermates during differential center motion (WT n = 8, VGluT3−/− n = 9, p < 0.02), but not global or differential surround motion (p > 0.1 for both).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing WT and VGluT3−/− mice

claim: W3-RGC EPSCs in VGluT3−/− mice were not altered during global or differential surround motion compared to WT.
source: W3-RGC EPSCs in VGluT3−/− mice were significantly reduced compared to WT littermates during differential center motion (WT n = 8, VGluT3−/− n = 9, p < 0.02), but not global or differential surround motion (p > 0.1 for both).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing WT and VGluT3−/− mice

claim: Spike responses of W3-RGCs were decreased for differential center motion in VGluT3−/− mice compared to WT.
source: A similar pattern was observed in the spike responses of W3-RGCs, which were decreased for differential center motion (WT n = 13, VGluT3−/− n = 9, p < 0.001), but not altered during global image motion (p > 0.9).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing WT and VGluT3−/− mice

claim: Spike responses of W3-RGCs during global image motion were not altered in VGluT3−/− mice compared to WT.
source: A similar pattern was observed in the spike responses of W3-RGCs, which were decreased for differential center motion (WT n = 13, VGluT3−/− n = 9, p < 0.001), but not altered during global image motion (p > 0.9).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing WT and VGluT3−/− mice

claim: Excitatory inputs and spike responses of W3-RGCs were reduced for narrow bars in VGluT3−/− mice.
source: Whereas excitatory inputs and spike responses were reduced for narrow bars (excitation at 100 μm, WT n = 6, VGluT3−/− n = 6, p < 0.03, spikes at 100 μm, WT n = 14, VGluT3−/− n = 8, p < 0.01), they did not differ significantly for bars of greater heights (excitation at 600 μm, WT n = 6, VGluT3−/− n = 6, p > 0.6, spikes at 600 μm, WT n = 14, VGluT3−/− n = 8, p < 0.2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing WT and VGluT3−/− mice

claim: Excitatory inputs and spike responses of W3-RGCs did not differ significantly for bars of greater heights in VGluT3−/− mice compared to WT.
source: Whereas excitatory inputs and spike responses were reduced for narrow bars (excitation at 100 μm, WT n = 6, VGluT3−/− n = 6, p < 0.03, spikes at 100 μm, WT n = 14, VGluT3−/− n = 8, p < 0.01), they did not differ significantly for bars of greater heights (excitation at 600 μm, WT n = 6, VGluT3−/− n = 6, p > 0.6, spikes at 600 μm, WT n = 14, VGluT3−/− n = 8, p < 0.2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing WT and VGluT3−/− mice

claim: VG3-ACs provide approximately half of the excitatory input to W3-RGCs.
source: In agreement with anatomical results (Figure 4B,C), VG3-ACs, thus, appear to provide approximately half of the excitatory input to W3-RGCs.
evidence: Inferred from VGluT3 knockout data showing ~50% reduction in EPSCs

claim: Feature selectivity of VG3-input is more sharply tuned than the excitatory input remaining in VGluT3−/− mice.
source: Importantly, feature selectivity of this VG3-input is more sharply tuned than the excitatory input remaining in VGluT3−/− mice—likely provided by ON and OFF bipolar cells—and is required for normal spike responses of W3-RGCs.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of response properties in WT and VGluT3−/− mice

claim: The excitatory input remaining in VGluT3−/− mice is likely provided by ON and OFF bipolar cells.
source: Importantly, feature selectivity of this VG3-input is more sharply tuned than the excitatory input remaining in VGluT3−/− mice—likely provided by ON and OFF bipolar cells—and is required for normal spike responses of W3-RGCs.
evidence: Inferred from knowledge of retinal circuitry and experimental results

claim: VG3-input is required for normal spike responses of W3-RGCs.
source: Importantly, feature selectivity of this VG3-input is more sharply tuned than the excitatory input remaining in VGluT3−/− mice—likely provided by ON and OFF bipolar cells—and is required for normal spike responses of W3-RGCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced spike responses in VGluT3−/− mice

claim: VG3-ACs serve to amplify and sharpen the tuning of responses to object motion in the OMS circuit.
source: In the OMS circuit (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), VG3-ACs serve to amplify and sharpen the tuning of responses to object motion.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing VG3-ACs have sharper tuning than bipolar cell input

claim: Surround inhibition acts at three levels: bipolar axon terminals, VG3-ACs, and W3-RGCs.
source: Surround inhibition acts at three levels: bipolar axon terminals, VG3-ACs, and W3-RGCs (Zhang et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2012 and Lee et al., 2014

claim: The added level of inhibition onto VG3-ACs compared to conventional pathways likely contributes to the more complete surround suppression in the OMS circuit.
source: The added level of inhibition onto VG3-ACs compared to conventional pathways through bipolar cells likely contributes to the more complete surround suppression in the OMS circuit.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about circuit function based on experimental observations

claim: Channeling of excitation through VG3-ACs introduces a delay not shared by the inhibitory input.
source: Moreover, channeling of excitation through VG3-ACs introduces a delay not shared by the inhibitory input, which could improve cancellation of center signals by the surround, for example, during global image motion.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about temporal dynamics of the circuit

claim: The sequential arrangement of three thresholding nonlinearities likely contributes to increasing selectivity at successive stages of the OMS circuit.
source: The sequential arrangement of three thresholding nonlinearities—glutamate release from bipolar cells, glutamate release from VG3-ACs, and spike generation in W3-RGCs—likely further contributes to the increasing selectivity for narrow vs broad edges and differential center vs global texture motion at successive stages of the OMS circuit.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about how circuit architecture contributes to feature selectivity

claim: The diversity of AC types and circuit motifs are integral to the diversity of features encoded in signals the retina sends to the brain.
source: Finally, our results support the notion that the diversity of AC types and circuit motifs in which they participate are integral to the diversity of features encoded in the signals the retinal sends to the brain (Masland, 2012; Jadzinsky and Baccus, 2013).
evidence: Supported by experimental results and citations to Masland, 2012 and Jadzinsky and Baccus, 2013

claim: VG3-ACs are arranged in regular mosaics with characteristic exclusion zones.
source: Density recovery profiles for tdTomato (n = 17 retinas) and VGluT3 (n = 10 retinas) signals in images like that shown in (A) from VG3-Cre Ai9 mice showed that VG3-ACs are arranged in regular mosaics with characteristic exclusion zones in their density recovery profiles (average densities VGluT3: 898 ± 34 cells/mm2, n = 10 retinas, tdTomato: 948 ± 37 cells/mm2, n = 17 retinas, effective radii of exclusion zones VGluT3: 18.1 ± 1.8 μm, tdTomato: 16.9 ± 0.4 μm) (Rodieck, 1991).
evidence: Supported by density recovery profile analysis and citation to Rodieck, 1991

claim: The average density of VGluT3-positive cells is 898 ± 34 cells/mm².
source: Density recovery profiles for tdTomato (n = 17 retinas) and VGluT3 (n = 10 retinas) signals in images like that shown in (A) from VG3-Cre Ai9 mice showed that VG3-ACs are arranged in regular mosaics with characteristic exclusion zones in their density recovery profiles (average densities VGluT3: 898 ± 34 cells/mm2, n = 10 retinas, tdTomato: 948 ± 37 cells/mm2, n = 17 retinas, effective radii of exclusion zones VGluT3: 18.1 ± 1.8 μm, tdTomato: 16.9 ± 0.4 μm) (Rodieck, 1991).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements from 10 retinas

claim: The effective radius of exclusion zones for VGluT3-positive cells is 18.1 ± 1.8 μm.
source: Density recovery profiles for tdTomato (n = 17 retinas) and VGluT3 (n = 10 retinas) signals in images like that shown in (A) from VG3-Cre Ai9 mice showed that VG3-ACs are arranged in regular mosaics with characteristic exclusion zones in their density recovery profiles (average densities VGluT3: 898 ± 34 cells/mm2, n = 10 retinas, tdTomato: 948 ± 37 cells/mm2, n = 17 retinas, effective radii of exclusion zones VGluT3: 18.1 ± 1.8 μm, tdTomato: 16.9 ± 0.4 μm) (Rodieck, 1991).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements from 10 retinas

claim: VG3-ACs stratify in sublamina 2 and 3 of the IPL.
source: Intensity profiles (mean ± SEM, n = 10 retinas) of these labels show that VG3-ACs stratify in sublamina 2 and 3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3) of the IPLs, the boundaries of which are marked by Calretinin (Wassle, 2004).
evidence: Supported by intensity profile analysis and citation to Wassle, 2004

claim: Stratification in sublamina 2 and 3 positions VG3-ACs ideally to recruit input from transient rectified ON and OFF bipolar cells.
source: Stratification in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3, thus, positions VG3-ACs ideally to recruit input from transient rectified ON and OFF bipolar cells, as well as to form synapses with dendrites of W3-RGCs.
evidence: Inferred from knowledge of bipolar cell stratification patterns and VG3-AC laminar position

claim: In all species examined, VG3-ACs and LED RGCs stratify near the center of the IPL.
source: The strategic importance of this laminar position is further corroborated by the observation that in all species examined, VG3-ACs and LED RGCs stratify near the center of the IPL (Berson et al., 1998; Roska and Werblin, 2001; Famiglietti, 2005; van Wyk et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies across species

claim: Peak times of ON and OFF filters were not significantly different for voltage, excitation, and inhibition in VG3-ACs.
source: Peak times of ON and OFF filters were not significantly different for voltage (B, black, n = 9, p > 0.2), excitation (F, red, n = 9, p > 0.4), and inhibition (J, blue, n = 9, p > 0.08).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from white noise analysis

claim: ON filters were more biphasic than OFF filters for excitation and inhibition in VG3-ACs.
source: However, ON filters were more biphasic than OFF filters for excitation (G, red, p < 0.002) and inhibition (K, blue, p < 0.002), but not voltage responses (B, black, p > 0.1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from white noise analysis

claim: VG3-ACs and their synaptic inputs show higher sensitivity to OFF compared to ON stimuli.
source: Temporal frequency tuning functions calculated from Fourier amplitudes of ON (left panels) and OFF (right panels) filters for voltage (D, black), excitation (H, red), and inhibition (L, blue) responses show response suppression at high- and low-stimulus frequencies and illustrate the higher sensitivity of VG3-ACs and their synaptic inputs to OFF compared to ON stimuli.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from temporal frequency tuning analysis

claim: Removal of VGluT3 affected neither gross morphological development of the retina nor dendritic patterns of W3-RGCs.
source: Removal of VGluT3, which in the retina is only expressed by VG3-ACs, affected neither gross morphological development of the retina (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) nor dendritic patterns of W3-RGCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by anatomical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and 3

claim: VGluT3 in the retina is only expressed by VG3-ACs.
source: Removal of VGluT3, which in the retina is only expressed by VG3-ACs, affected neither gross morphological development of the retina (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) nor dendritic patterns of W3-RGCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Represents established knowledge about VGluT3 expression in the retina

claim: EPSCs elicited by differential center motion were reduced by approximately 50% in W3-RGCs of VGluT3−/− compared to wild-type mice.
source: EPSCs elicited by differential center motion were reduced by approximately 50% in W3-RGCs of VGluT3−/− compared to wild-type (WT) mice (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E,F

claim: Excitation during global motion and tonic excitation revealed by differential surround stimulation were unchanged in VGluT3−/− mice.
source: By contrast, excitation during global motion and tonic excitation revealed by differential surround stimulation were unchanged.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing WT and VGluT3−/− mice

claim: EPSCs and spike responses evoked by edges of narrow moving bars were suppressed across a wide range of speeds in VGluT3−/− mice.
source: Similarly, EPSCs and spike responses evoked by edges of narrow moving bars (height: 100 μm) were suppressed across a wide range of speeds in VGluT3−/− mice (Figure 4I–L and data not shown), whereas excitation and spike responses elicited by broader moving bars remained intact in VGluT3−/− mice (Figure 4I–L).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I-L

claim: Excitation and spike responses elicited by broader moving bars remained intact in VGluT3−/− mice.
source: Similarly, EPSCs and spike responses evoked by edges of narrow moving bars (height: 100 μm) were suppressed across a wide range of speeds in VGluT3−/− mice (Figure 4I–L and data not shown), whereas excitation and spike responses elicited by broader moving bars remained intact in VGluT3−/− mice (Figure 4I–L).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I-L

claim: Multi-tiered inhibition combined with delayed excitation, and successive threshold nonlinearities likely contribute to sharpening of object motion tuning.
source: Multi-tiered inhibition combined with delayed excitation, and successive threshold nonlinearities likely contribute to sharpening.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about circuit mechanisms based on experimental observations

claim: Inhibition in the OMS circuit is provided by a single AC type or a shared set of AC types.
source: Key features—transient ON and OFF input driven by rectified subunits—are similar at all three stages, arguing that inhibition is provided by a single AC type or a shared set of AC types, which remain to be identified.
evidence: Inferred from similarity of inhibitory properties at different circuit stages

claim: The inhibitory amacrine cell types providing surround inhibition in the OMS circuit remain to be identified.
source: Key features—transient ON and OFF input driven by rectified subunits—are similar at all three stages, arguing that inhibition is provided by a single AC type or a shared set of AC types, which remain to be identified.
evidence: Explicit statement about unknown circuit components
